- `backend_asynchronous_multi_qpu` (simulation_backends): The single-workload half that was absent now exists, and the row is partial because the other half is what CUDA-Q actually claims. `flagquantum.remote.jobs.submit_to_targets` takes one program and a sequence of targets, materializes it to an IR once before any target is contacted, hands each target its own submission to a thread pool, and returns without waiting. Every target gets the `RemoteJob` the single-target `submit` returns -- its own status, wait, result, cancel, and private receipt -- so the streams progress independently and are read independently, and the report lists targets in the order the caller named them rather than in the order the network answered. A target that refuses the program is recorded with its exception type and message against that target, and the others still submit; a failed submission is never retried, because an ambiguous submission may already have reached a provider. An unreadable program, a non-sequence `targets`, an empty list, a repeated target, and a `name` that would have to name several submissions are all refused before any target is contacted, and the refusal is argued for by a submission count of zero rather than by a message. What is absent is the half CUDA-Q's own name for the option states: this is fan-out, not one partitioned workload. Every target runs a full copy of the program, no state, shot, or sample crosses targets, and nothing combines the independent streams into one estimate, so the report declares `distribution_semantics = replicated_independent_targets` and `scalability_claim_allowed = False` with its three blockers, and deliberately carries no `world_size`, `local_world_size`, `node_count`, or rank ownership, because there is no rank to attribute anything to. The function is not re-exported from `flagquantum.remote` and no root name was added. - `dynamics_schedule_and_integrators` (simulation_backends): The integrator family is selectable and the selection is measured, but the generator it integrates is static. `flagquantum/simulation/lindblad_integrators.py` declares three schemes -- explicit fourth-order Runge-Kutta, the second-order implicit Crank-Nicolson trapezoidal rule and a matrix-free Krylov exponential -- and publishes them as `flagquantum.lindblad.INTEGRATOR_NAMES`; all three are reachable through the `method=` argument of `flagquantum.lindblad.run`, `.plan` and `.adjoint_gradient`, with `solve_tolerance` setting the Krylov precision, an unknown name refused rather than substituted, and the exponential scheme reporting no step order because on a time-independent generator it has none. `tests/unit/test_lindblad_integrators.py` measures that partition rather than asserting it: the vocabulary is closed, an unknown method is refused by both the planner and the integrator, the method that ran is the method that was reported, and the implicit scheme stays bounded and refines toward the exact stiff solution where the explicit one diverges. - `batched_trajectory` (noise_and_error_models): Trajectory simulation exists; batched execution across trajectories is narrower than the baseline.
- `unitary_mixture_degradation` (noise_and_error_models): The distinction is made in the noise layer and is decided by the operators rather than by the channel's name: `KrausChannel.unitary_mixture` reports the branches and their weights, and the criterion is that every operator is a non-negative real scale times a unitary, with the whole Gram matrix checked rather than its leading entry, so an amplitude damping channel is refused for its unequal singular values. A zero-weight operator is a branch of probability zero and is dropped rather than read as a general channel, so every built-in factory stays classified at the edges of its range. Three reading sites consume the answer. The stabilizer positioned-noise entry point executes a one- or two-wire channel whose branches are Pauli frames and refuses every other channel by name, so a depolarizing channel samples as its four frames where it previously refused, and the stabilizer survey reports that same verdict without executing the program. And the batched statevector trajectory kernel asks the classifier rather than the opcode table, so a channel that table never listed -- the two-qubit depolarizing channel, or any channel a caller writes -- draws one branch per trajectory row against the channel's own weights and applies only the branches it drew, where a channel that is not a mixture keeps the general Kraus kernel. The two routes count their events separately, so which estimator ran a channel is read rather than assumed, and they are the same estimator: on this box both return bit-identical states at the same seeds, so the classification buys cost and not a different distribution. Two limits keep the row partial. The framework comparison gives no Python accessor for the property at all, so there is no external surface to conform against and the contract here is FlagQuantum's own. And the classification changes a route only where a route has a choice to make: the exact density-matrix route sums the whole channel whether or not it is a mixture, so the density-matrix route is the one place the answer cannot be used, and no planning or scheduling decision here is taken from it. The audit measured the reading sites rather than counting them, and the count in the reason above is exact: `unitary_mixture` occurs in exactly three files under `flagquantum/` -- it is defined at `flagquantum/noise/channels.py:236` with `is_unitary_mixture` at `:276`, and it is read at `flagquantum/simulation/stabilizer/engine.py:744` and in `flagquantum/simulation/statevector/noisy.py`. The token's own claim was measured separately from that: `unitary_mixture` occurs zero times under `flagquantum/runtime/planner/` and zero times under `flagquantum/compiler/`, so no planning or compilation decision is taken from the classification and the token stands as written.
- `noise_trajectory_shot_allocation` (noise_and_error_models): FlagQuantum samples Kraus trajectories, but the trajectory choice belongs to the engine rather than to the caller: the MPS trajectory path draws them implicitly and exposes an ensemble size, so there is no trajectory enumeration and no ordered or probabilistic selection strategy, and the strategy half is the whole of this row. The allocation half of that sentence is narrower than it reads: the planner does state how many trajectories a precision target asks for -- `flagquantum/runtime/planner/noise_selection.py:191` computes a required count from `target_standard_error`, and the block opened at `:177` folds a pilot variance and a confidence level into it first, and it is reported as `estimated_trajectories_to_target` and pinned by `tests/test_noise.py:1320` and `:1381` -- so what is absent is not the count but the policy that spends it, because nothing here allocates a run's trajectories or shots from that requirement and the count is used for candidate cost and feasibility rather than for execution. Those strategies are the whole of this row.
- `fermion_operator_algebra` (operator_algebra_and_domain_libraries): The algebra and two mappings exist. `flagquantum/observables/fermion.py` builds a normal-ordered sum over spin orbitals with `create`, `annihilate`, and `number`; addition, subtraction, unary negation, scalar multiplication, `*`, `dagger`, `commutator`, and `anticommutator` are all present, so a chemistry workload's generator is an expression rather than a hand-applied relation, and equality is structural, which makes `is_hermitian` exact rather than a tolerance test. Two transforms map a Hermitian operator to the Pauli `Observable` the existing statevector path already measures: `jordan_wigner`, whose Z string runs over the modes strictly below a factor's mode, and `parity_encoding`, whose X string runs over the modes strictly above it. The two images are the same operator in two qubit bases - the parity image is the Jordan-Wigner image conjugated by the change of basis from occupation to parity, which the focused tests check against the Jordan-Wigner image rather than against a hand-written table - so what the second encoding changes is where the image is local, not how wide its widest term is. The widest factor image still costs one wire per mode under both, reached at opposite ends of the mode list, and the reduction in Pauli weight that is the reason Bravyi-Kitaev and ternary-tree encodings exist follows from neither, so those two remain absent and are still an owned gap. The mode count is an argument rather than inferred, and no matrix form of a fermionic operator ships. The audit measured where the two absent names sit: Bravyi-Kitaev and ternary-tree occur in the file exactly once and only as motivation, in the docstring naming them as what the worst-case Pauli weight is measured against, so no function, constant, or parameter offers either and both mappings that ship pay the linear Z string.
- `matrix_and_custom_operator` (operator_algebra_and_domain_libraries): A stable operator schema and discovery interface exist, and a matrix can now enter the superoperator algebra as a term factor. What is still missing is a matrix-valued operator type in the operator algebra itself: no `MatrixOperator` or `custom_op` type composes with `Observable` or the fermionic sum through products, sums, scalars, adjoints, or commutators, and the superoperator factor contract is deliberately narrower than that, requiring only `__matmul__`, `__rmatmul__` and `dense()`. The audit re-measured the absence as a name search and as a role search. The names are absent: neither `MatrixOperator` nor any class or function whose name joins a matrix with the word operator occurs under `flagquantum/`. The role is not unserved, and that is what the token is careful about: a raw matrix enters a program as a value rather than as an algebra member -- `Circuit.any` carries a unitary as a matrix instruction, and `flagquantum/simulation/density_matrix.py` exports `apply_unitary_density` and `expand_operator` to act with one -- so the row is about a matrix-valued *operator type* that joins the observable or fermion algebra, not about whether a matrix can reach a circuit.
- `exponential_pauli_operator` (operator_algebra_and_domain_libraries): The dense constructor exists: `flagquantum/simulation/pauli.py` reads a Pauli word and its targets positionally, so character `i` of the word acts on `targets[i]`, and returns the operator the pair denotes on a declared number of wires. A Pauli product squares to the identity, so the exponential is evaluated in closed form as `exp(-i theta P) = cos(theta) I - i sin(theta) P` rather than by exponentiating a matrix; the form is exact at every angle and is checked against an eigendecomposition of the product and against the defining series of the exponential. An `I` character consumes its target and contributes no support, so a word aligns with a wire list without dropping the wires it does not act on, and an all-identity word returns the global phase it denotes instead of the identity. A word whose length disagrees with the number of targets, a character outside `X`, `Y`, `Z` and `I`, a repeated target, a target outside the declared wires, and a non-finite angle are each refused. What is absent is the circuit-level form, and it is the whole of the row: no operation the IR carries and no compiler pattern decomposes it into single-qubit basis changes and a CNOT chain, so a circuit cannot contain an exponential of a Pauli product, no rotation parameter reaches it as a differentiable value, and `pauli_word` is not a value type a kernel parameter can be written with. The dense constructor is the operator those three would be built from. The audit measured the three clauses one at a time. The IR clause is a table lookup and holds: `flagquantum/core/operator_schema.py` declares 35 opcodes and none of them carries `pauli` or `exp` in its name, so there is no circuit-level operation to emit. The decomposition clause holds by the same table: nothing in `flagquantum/compiler/` can decompose an operation the schema table does not admit. The structural value types the private kernel IR carries are `IRType` instances built in `flagquantum/compiler/_hybrid/model.py:40`, and no Pauli-word type is among them, which is the measurement behind the third clause.
- `state_and_unitary_access` (algorithm_layer): Circuit.state exists. A full unitary accessor is absent.
- `algorithm_block_encoding_family` (algorithm_layer): Three members of the family are implemented natively and the rest are absent. Trotter time evolution landed as flagquantum.algorithms.trotter: a weighted Pauli sum becomes an ordinary Circuit through a product formula of order 1 or 2, with the exact circuit for one Pauli word's exponential as its primitive. Block encoding landed next as flagquantum.algorithms.primitives.block_encoding, promoted out of the private helper flagquantum.algorithms.svd held, and it carries the qubitization walk step with it: the reflection is emitted as one dense matrix, the flagged block is the matrix over the caller's subnormalisation, and one walk step is a rotation whose eigenphases are the arccosines of the encoded eigenvalues. The fermion-qubit transform family already had jordan_wigner at flagquantum.observables.fermion. A third member landed as flagquantum.algorithms.primitives.linear_combination, the Pauli linear-combination encoding: a Hamiltonian given as a weighted sum of Pauli words is encoded from its coefficients rather than from a matrix, at the sum of the coefficient magnitudes as the stated subnormalisation, and it satisfies the same two protocols the spectral encoding satisfies, so one consumer reads either without being told which it holds. The row names three registry entries because the shipped members are separate capabilities with separate surfaces and separate evidence: the product formula, the spectral block encoding, and the Pauli linear-combination encoding that is a second implementation behind the spectral encoding's own two protocols. The plan's original route -- adapt Qualtran, Apache-2.0, which covers the same mathematics -- was ruled out by the repository owner: Qualtran 0.7.0 carries 27 transitive dependencies and is not declared in dependency-policy.toml, so the mathematics is implemented natively instead and no third-party quantum-algorithm library is a dependency.

NelderMead is implemented as the deterministic counterpart: it reads only the order of objective values, so it needs no perturbation size and no random draw, and its result reports the two spreads the run stopped on beside a converged flag that says a simplex collapsed rather than that the point is a global minimum. The two units are disjoint in scope rather than redundant, and the pair is why the row now names two registry entries: SPSA is for a sampled objective and Nelder-Mead is defeated by one. What keeps the row short of `supported` is the integration the route lands on, and the guide names both halves of it. The first is the `^` separator: the default reading states the line as written and is not graphlike, so both registered decoders refuse it -- 113 of the 219 mechanisms of a distance-3, two-round rotated surface code flip more than two detectors -- while the reading a matcher accepts, use_decomp_suggestions=True followed by merge_duplicate_mechanisms(), is measurably a different distribution, because against stim's own sampler at 200000 shots the default reading's observable marginal sits 2.1 standard errors away and the graphlike reading's sits 56. The guide reports both numbers, names the default reading as the model for a threshold or a marginal and the graphlike one as the model for a matcher, and shows that a decoded logical error rate at this distance does not separate the two routes while the per-shot agreement does: the in-tree matcher and the PyMatching cross-check agree on every shot and belief propagation with ordered statistics differs on 1.7 percent of them. The second half is the registry: belief propagation with ordered statistics decodes a hyperedge model and is reachable from the package, but register_decoder requires a from_detector_error_model classmethod that class does not carry, so decoder_names() holds the matcher and the cross-check alone and a hyperedge model has no name to ask for. Both are stated as boundaries in the guide, which is what makes this documentation work rather than a page that stops where the implementation does. The audit made the token's subject explicit because this row is the one place in the contract where a `search:` body states an absence in another product rather than in this tree, and the two are not interchangeable here: a reader who greps this repository for the page finds it at `docs/guides/STIM_USER_MIGRATION.md` and for the writer finds `DetectorErrorModel.to_stim_text` at `flagquantum/qec/dem.py:1138`, the reader being `from_stim_text` at `:885`. `flagquantum/qec/registry.py:257` is the decoder-side consumer of the reader. The upstream reading the token now names is the one `docs/development/CUDAQ_PARITY_BASELINE.md:142` tables, which attributes the for-Stim-users page to the CUDA-Q Logical preview layer and records that cudaq-qec publishes none; that attribution is a statement about the upstream products and is not measurable from this tree, which is precisely why it must not be left looking like a statement about this one.
- `logical_resource_estimation` (logical_and_ftqc_layer): A rotated-surface-code cost over the compiler's own static estimate rather than a second tally: flagquantum.algorithms.logical_resources reads the operation counts, the T family, and the schedule depth from flagquantum.compiler.resource_estimation.estimate_resources and adds the code layer, at a distance the caller names, as 2 d^2 - 1 physical qubits per patch and d surface-code cycles per logical layer. The row is partial for three named reasons. The input has to already be Clifford+T: a parametric rotation is refused rather than synthesised, because this unit reads opcodes and runs no legalization, so a T-count taken over a rotation the program still contains would be the count of a circuit nobody will run -- an exact quarter turn has a Clifford+T form in the compiler now, and this unit does not reach it -- and a compound operation whose T-count is its decomposition's -- a Toffoli, a controlled swap -- is refused, because a Toffoli is not a Clifford gate and the decompositions do not agree on what it costs. There is no distillation factory, magic-state budget, routing overhead, placement, scheduling, or device model, so the physical figure is a floor for a circuit of these layers rather than a compiled estimate. And no logical error rate is reported, because a threshold fit's prefactor and threshold are a device's numbers rather than this unit's. Reaching the compiler's own quarter-turn table from this unit, angle synthesis for an arbitrary angle, and the arithmetic constructions are the moves that would take this row to supported.
- `arithmetic_bloqs` (logical_and_ftqc_layer): A reversible in-place ripple-carry adder, and it is Cuccaro's construction rather than the Gidney-Ekera one this row is named for. flagquantum.algorithms.arithmetic builds it for a width the caller names: 2 n Toffolis and 6 n + 1 cx, 8 n + 1 operations on 2 n + 2 wires, linear in the width and independent of the addends, with one working carry wire that the circuit restores and a carry-out wire left holding the carry out of the most significant position. Those two wires must enter holding zero, and only inputs meeting that contract are promised a sum: the map is a permutation of the whole space, so an off-contract input is reversible and is not the sum, and the row is partial rather than supported partly because that restriction is real rather than incidental. The row is also partial because the construction is narrower than the surface it is measured against. Both addends are quantum registers, so there is no classical addend, no add_constant, no modular adder, no controlled adder, no comparison, no multiplier, and no modular exponentiation, and there is no carry-in parameter. No seven-T expansion is written beside the circuit: the T-count is the compiler's own Toffoli rule, ccx lowering to the fifteen-gate h, t, tdg, cx identity in flagquantum.compiler.basis_translation and reaching the report through convert_basis plus flagquantum.compiler.resource_estimation.estimate_resources and flagquantum.algorithms.logical_resources, so the two numbers cannot disagree but the arithmetic is not cheaper than the compiler makes it. What is absent is owned rather than implied: the Gidney-Ekera construction is smaller precisely because it uncomputes its ancillas by measuring them and feeding the outcomes forward, which needs a mid-circuit measurement and a classical feedforward path this repository has no costable circuit for, so writing it is the move that would complete this row rather than a variant of what landed. The Qualtran adaptation that was once the planned route is not the route that was taken, and no Qualtran dependency was added for an adder to reuse.

What is absent is the operator type the CUDA-Q surface builds a channel from: no matrix-valued operator participates in operator algebra, which is the gap `matrix_and_custom_operator` already records. |
| `noise_model_callback` | Noise model callbacks injecting noise by operation type at runtime | partial | next | none | `noisy_simulation` | Per-gate (`NoiseModel.add(gate_names, channel)`) and per-qubit (`wires=`) static injection both exist, and lowering now refuses a rule that cannot apply. The callback form is absent, and `NoiseRule` carries a `KrausChannel` fixed at construction. A callback cannot be added to `NoiseRule` as it stands: `NoiseModel.identity` is a SHA-256 digest of `to_dict()`, and checkpoint resume and execution-plan identity both bind to it, so a channel chosen by an arbitrary callable would make identity unreproducible. Any such rule must be registered under a declared name and parameterization before it can participate in a model identity. |

The model can also state that mechanisms are alternatives rather than independent, which is the one thing its parity matrices cannot carry: an error id groups them, the marginal rates and the sampler read a group as one fault, and the text writer refuses an id-carrying model instead of printing an independent one under the same probabilities. The row stays partial because conversion is narrower than the baseline at the input end: `from_memory_circuit` accepts one circuit record and one noise record, so an arbitrary circuit carrying detector and observable annotations has no route to a model, and a non-Pauli channel is refused rather than decomposed. The output end is no longer one of the limits: `circuit_from_detector_error_model` writes a model as the detector-level realization it already is and `detector_error_model_from_circuit` reads it back exactly, error ids included, so a model reaches the stabilizer engine without a statevector and without a second construction. What that route does not and cannot return is the circuit the model was built from, because a model states which detector parities a fault flips and never which measurements compose a detector; it returns the canonical detector-level circuit every model determines, with the detector count stated by the caller. `flagquantum/qec/IMPLEMENTATION.md` records the sweeps, the arithmetic and the realization. The audit confirmed this absence and now cites the refusal that states it: `flagquantum/qec/dem_circuit.py:199` reads a circuit back into the model it realizes, but only for a circuit `circuit_from_detector_error_model` built, and `:209` gives the reason in its own words -- it states what a realization is rather than guessing at what an arbitrary annotated circuit might mean. The reader's preconditions are the shape of the absence: every instruction a fault frame or a measurement, measurements one per wire in wire order and after every frame, and every wire a frame names flipped by one of its branches. An annotated circuit from elsewhere satisfies none of them and is refused rather than interpreted. |
| `unitary_mixture_degradation` | Unitary-mixture noise models distinguished from general channels | partial | next | none | `noisy_simulation` | The distinction is made in the noise layer and is decided by the operators rather than by the channel's name: `KrausChannel.unitary_mixture` reports the branches and their weights, and the criterion is that every operator is a non-negative real scale times a unitary, with the whole Gram matrix checked rather than its leading entry, so an amplitude damping channel is refused for its unequal singular values. A zero-weight operator is a branch of probability zero and is dropped rather than read as a general channel, so every built-in factory stays classified at the edges of its range. Three reading sites consume the answer. The stabilizer positioned-noise entry point executes a one- or two-wire channel whose branches are Pauli frames and refuses every other channel by name, so a depolarizing channel samples as its four frames where it previously refused, and the stabilizer survey reports that same verdict without executing the program. And the batched statevector trajectory kernel asks the classifier rather than the opcode table, so a channel that table never listed -- the two-qubit depolarizing channel, or any channel a caller writes -- draws one branch per trajectory row against the channel's own weights and applies only the branches it drew, where a channel that is not a mixture keeps the general Kraus kernel. The two routes count their events separately, so which estimator ran a channel is read rather than assumed, and they are the same estimator: on this box both return bit-identical states at the same seeds, so the classification buys cost and not a different distribution. Two limits keep the row partial. The framework comparison gives no Python accessor for the property at all, so there is no external surface to conform against and the contract here is FlagQuantum's own. And the classification changes a route only where a route has a choice to make: the exact density-matrix route sums the whole channel whether or not it is a mixture, so the density-matrix route is the one place the answer cannot be used, and no planning or scheduling decision here is taken from it. The audit measured the reading sites rather than counting them, and the count in the reason above is exact: `unitary_mixture` occurs in exactly three files under `flagquantum/` -- it is defined at `flagquantum/noise/channels.py:236` with `is_unitary_mixture` at `:276`, and it is read at `flagquantum/simulation/stabilizer/engine.py:744` and in `flagquantum/simulation/statevector/noisy.py`. The token's own claim was measured separately from that: `unitary_mixture` occurs zero times under `flagquantum/runtime/planner/` and zero times under `flagquantum/compiler/`, so no planning or compilation decision is taken from the classification and the token stands as written. |
| `noise_trajectory_shot_allocation` | The ptsbe trajectory engine: explicit Kraus trajectory specification, exhaustive, ordered, and probabilistic trajectory sampling strategies, and shot allocation across trajectories | partial | next | none | `noisy_simulation` | FlagQuantum samples Kraus trajectories, but the trajectory choice belongs to the engine rather than to the caller: the MPS trajectory path draws them implicitly and exposes an ensemble size, so there is no trajectory enumeration and no ordered or probabilistic selection strategy, and the strategy half is the whole of this row. The allocation half of that sentence is narrower than it reads: the planner does state how many trajectories a precision target asks for -- `flagquantum/runtime/planner/noise_selection.py:191` computes a required count from `target_standard_error`, and the block opened at `:177` folds a pilot variance and a confidence level into it first, and it is reported as `estimated_trajectories_to_target` and pinned by `tests/test_noise.py:1320` and `:1381` -- so what is absent is not the count but the policy that spends it, because nothing here allocates a run's trajectories or shots from that requirement and the count is used for candidate cost and feasibility rather than for execution. Those strategies are the whole of this row. |

#### Operator algebra and domain libraries

Domain id: `operator_algebra_and_domain_libraries`

CUDA-Q surface: SpinOperator, FermionOperator, BosonOperator, SuperOperator, MatrixOperator, operator arithmetics, pauli_word and exp_pauli, chemistry libraries

| Capability | CUDA-Q baseline | Status | Priority | Dependency class | FlagQuantum maturity | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `spin_operator_algebra` | SpinOperator and Pauli operator algebra | partial | now | none | `ir` | The earlier reason overstated the gap and is replaced by measurement. Products, sums, and scalars are not absent: Observable in flagquantum/observables/__init__.py implements __add__, __sub__, __mul__, __rmul__, __neg__, and __matmul__, and each returns an Observable rather than a matrix, so X(0) + Z(0) is an Observable carrying two terms and 2 * X(0), X(0) * 2, X(0) - Z(0), X(0) @ Y(1), and -X(0) are all Observables. What is genuinely absent on the Pauli side is four operations: commutator, anticommutator, exponential together with its exp spelling, and __pow__. Each of the first three raises AttributeError and X(0) ** 2 raises TypeError, so no commutator and no exponential of a Pauli sum can be taken. The same package already gives the fermionic and bosonic siblings their commutators, FermionOperator.commutator and FermionOperator.anticommutator in flagquantum/observables/fermion.py and BosonOperator.commutator and BosonOperator.anticommutator in flagquantum/observables/boson.py, so the gap is a Pauli-side asymmetry rather than an absent algebra. Observable also exposes no dense or matrix accessor, so a caller who needs the matrix of a Pauli sum reaches PauliSum.dense or the simulation route instead. All four missing operations are additive members of Observable, which is one of the 36 names in the Stable Core export set, so closing this row is an API change under rule 8 with no approval today, and the row stays partial rather than partially built. |
| `fermion_operator_algebra` | FermionOperator with Jordan-Wigner and related mappings | partial | next | none | `observables_fermion_operator_algebra` | The algebra and two mappings exist. `flagquantum/observables/fermion.py` builds a normal-ordered sum over spin orbitals with `create`, `annihilate`, and `number`; addition, subtraction, unary negation, scalar multiplication, `*`, `dagger`, `commutator`, and `anticommutator` are all present, so a chemistry workload's generator is an expression rather than a hand-applied relation, and equality is structural, which makes `is_hermitian` exact rather than a tolerance test. Two transforms map a Hermitian operator to the Pauli `Observable` the existing statevector path already measures: `jordan_wigner`, whose Z string runs over the modes strictly below a factor's mode, and `parity_encoding`, whose X string runs over the modes strictly above it. The two images are the same operator in two qubit bases - the parity image is the Jordan-Wigner image conjugated by the change of basis from occupation to parity, which the focused tests check against the Jordan-Wigner image rather than against a hand-written table - so what the second encoding changes is where the image is local, not how wide its widest term is. The widest factor image still costs one wire per mode under both, reached at opposite ends of the mode list, and the reduction in Pauli weight that is the reason Bravyi-Kitaev and ternary-tree encodings exist follows from neither, so those two remain absent and are still an owned gap. The mode count is an argument rather than inferred, and no matrix form of a fermionic operator ships. Trotter time evolution landed as flagquantum.algorithms.trotter: a weighted Pauli sum becomes an ordinary Circuit through a product formula of order 1 or 2, with the exact circuit for one Pauli word's exponential as its primitive. Block encoding landed next as flagquantum.algorithms.primitives.block_encoding, promoted out of the private helper flagquantum.algorithms.svd held, and it carries the qubitization walk step with it: the reflection is emitted as one dense matrix, the flagged block is the matrix over the caller's subnormalisation, and one walk step is a rotation whose eigenphases are the arccosines of the encoded eigenvalues. The fermion-qubit transform family already had jordan_wigner at flagquantum.observables.fermion. A third member landed as flagquantum.algorithms.primitives.linear_combination, the Pauli linear-combination encoding: a Hamiltonian given as a weighted sum of Pauli words is encoded from its coefficients rather than from a matrix, at the sum of the coefficient magnitudes as the stated subnormalisation, and it satisfies the same two protocols the spectral encoding satisfies, so one consumer reads either without being told which it holds. Still absent: qubitization as a public walk object carrying a moment count, QSVT, double factorization, and the Bravyi-Kitaev, parity and ternary-tree transforms. The row names three registry entries because the shipped members are separate capabilities with separate surfaces and separate evidence: the product formula, the spectral block encoding, and the Pauli linear-combination encoding that is a second implementation behind the spectral encoding's own two protocols. The plan's original route -- adapt Qualtran, Apache-2.0, which covers the same mathematics -- was ruled out by the repository owner: Qualtran 0.7.0 carries 27 transitive dependencies and is not declared in dependency-policy.toml, so the mathematics is implemented natively instead and no third-party quantum-algorithm library is a dependency. |
| `error_mitigation` | Zero-noise extrapolation, probabilistic error cancellation, Clifford data regression, and readout-error mitigation | partial | now | none | `algorithms_zero_noise_extrapolation`, `algorithms_probabilistic_error_cancellation`, `algorithms_clifford_data_regression`, `algorithms_readout_error_mitigation`, `algorithms_gate_folding` | Zero-noise extrapolation, probabilistic error cancellation and Clifford data regression. An observable is measured at several error strengths by scaling the one error-probability parameter each noise channel declares, and the curve is continued to zero by polynomial least squares or Richardson extrapolation, which reports the residual it left and the variance amplification of its weights. The channel families whose parameters are not error probabilities are refused by name, and a model that declares a readout rule is refused rather than measured without it, because the estimate is Tr(O rho) and classical readout confusion is applied after measurement. Beside that, a channel the model declares as a Pauli channel is inverted exactly by decomposing its inverse into a signed combination of Pauli words read off its Pauli transfer matrix, one location at a time, which reports the sampling overhead gamma squared that a sampled implementation would pay and refuses by measured magnitude the channel families whose transfer matrix is not diagonal and the channels whose transfer eigenvalue reaches zero. The third member landed as flagquantum.algorithms.cdr: each phase, rx, ry, rz and u1 rotation of the target is snapped to its nearest quarter turn and rewritten into the named Clifford word for that turn, those training circuits' ideal values are read from exact density simulation and their noisy values from the same simulation of the declared model, and the affine relation between the two is fitted and applied to the target. Every training circuit is accepted by flagquantum.simulation.stabilizer.require_clifford_program before it is measured, so the membership that would make the training set cheap on hardware is enforced and never exploited: this path pays the target's own simulation cost and claims no capacity advantage from it, and it says so where the estimate is. A model that names an operation the rewrite removes is refused, because the model keys its channels on gate names and every training point would otherwise receive less noise than the target, and a program that declares a measurement or observable request is refused because the path reads Tr(O rho) and consumes no request. The fit's largest residual is the only diagnostic of the affine premise and is reported as absent rather than as an arithmetic zero when no degree of freedom was left, so a two-point fit's agreement is an identity rather than a check. The fourth member landed as flagquantum.algorithms.readout_mitigation, the leg the other three named as absent: the readout rules a NoiseModel declares are grouped into disjoint blocks, one block per rule, and each block's transpose inverse is applied to a measured distribution. The transposition is the index convention rather than a detail -- a calibration table is written with the true outcome as its row index while the vector the forward path produces has qubit 0 as its most significant bit -- and the two inverses differ by 0.14285714 in the maximum entry on ((0.9, 0.1), (0.2, 0.8)) and agree on a symmetric table, so the relation is asserted directly. A rule naming several qubits is inverted as one block because its marginals are a different operator, a qubit named by two rules is refused rather than confused twice, and a block whose smallest singular value reaches the declared floor is refused by measured magnitude rather than inverted into weights no shot count can support. The amplification the correction costs is the whole map's induced 1-norm, which for a map that is a tensor product of disjoint blocks is the product of the blocks' own rather than the worst block's, and the standard error a shot-based estimate inherits is that amplification over the square root of the count. The corrected vector is not forced onto the simplex: its negative mass is summed and reported beside it rather than clipped, because clipping would return a different vector under the same name. The fifth member landed as flagquantum.algorithms.folding, which reaches the scaled-noise curve without naming a channel parameter at all: the program is lengthened by an exact identity -- each instruction followed by its own inverse and then the instruction again, distributed one instruction at a time or as whole repeated bodies -- so the noise its instructions carry runs more times while nothing but the dtype's rounding changes what is computed, measured at 1.6e-16 on the five-instruction body h, cx, rz, ry, t at complex128 under both strategies. It is a different unit of scale rather than another scaling: what it reports is the length ratio it realized, that ratio is the abscissa the extrapolation fits against rather than the factor requested, and a call naming both a fold and a scaling callable is refused because the product of a length ratio and a channel parameter names neither. Two consequences are recorded rather than hidden. The circuit strategy repeats whole bodies so its realized ratio is 1 + 2m and a request of 1.4 is met by 3.0, while the gate strategy meets that same request exactly in seven instructions and meets 2.2 exactly in eleven where the circuit strategy's next reachable ratio, 3.0, costs it fifteen; and because both reach a ratio in steps of two instructions, two distinct requests can realize one length -- 1.4 and 2.6 both realize 3.0 on a body of five -- which is refused by naming the duplicated ratio rather than by failing inside the solve, since repeated abscissas make the linear system singular. A gate fold spends its pairs leftmost first, so a readout blind to where they land reads a flat curve over a program whose noise genuinely grew: with depolarizing at 0.03 on all five gates the added pair lands on the leading h and zz(0, 1) reads 0.672956129888 at both ratio 1.0 and ratio 1.4 while xx(0, 1) reads 0.242863810368 and 0.223823288052. The fold needs no noise model, which is what lets it run where a channel-scaling run is refused, but what it assumes instead -- that repeating an instruction repeats that instruction's error and changes no other instruction's error -- is a statement about crosstalk and drift that no program carries and no measurement here checks. What the family still does not carry: a tensored or sparse approximation for a block wider than the ceiling, any correction of a confusion the model does not declare, and any estimate of the noise a fold amplifies. |
| `variational_algorithms` | VQE and QAOA solver libraries | partial | now | none | `algorithms_variational_solvers`, `algorithms_vqe_solvers` | Both halves of the baseline's solver library are registered capabilities now, and the two entries are separate because their premises and their readings differ. The QAOA half landed as flagquantum.algorithms.variational and is registered as algorithms_variational_solvers: a weighted MaxCut edge list is checked once and reaches both the cost layer the ansatz applies and the operator the energy is scored against through the same tuple, which is the agreement the primitives beside it did not carry -- qaoa_circuit took edges and qaoa_loss took a Hamiltonian, and nothing related the two, so a caller could score one graph's ansatz against another graph's operator and read a number about a problem nobody posed. The operator is sum over edges of w_ij Z_i Z_j, whose value on a basis state is the edge total less twice the cut, and the entry point refuses a self-loop, a repeated undirected pair, a non-finite or non-real weight and an empty edge list by naming what a cost layer would have mishandled. The uniform superposition is an eigenstate of every cost and mixer term, so the gradient at a zero start is exactly zero at every layer count, which is why the start is a required argument rather than a default; a finite layer count is an approximation, so the energy is an expectation rather than a bound; and the fitted angles, the energy and the trajectory are all the result carries, with sampling, decoding and ranking left to the caller. The VQE half is the four entry points flagquantum.algorithms.core.run_vqe, run_adapt_vqe, run_hybrid_vqe and run_layerwise_vqe, which the examples, the services layer and the benchmarks already call. They are implemented and exercised -- tests/unit/test_vqe_optimizer_factory.py holds their optimizer-factory contract and tests/test_algorithms.py and tests/test_hybrid_optimization.py drive them on circuits -- and they are now a registered capability of their own, algorithms_vqe_solvers, with tests/unit/test_vqe_solvers.py as its focused unit and examples/algorithms/vqe_solvers.py as its golden path; that registration closed the first of the two things that kept this row partial. It did not close the second, the surface shape, and this row still does not claim the baseline's shape. The registration also settled two readings a caller could get wrong, recorded here because this row's evidence is what a reader reaches first. The ADAPT screen differentiates the objective at the appended angle and is therefore exact, so a reference state that is an eigenstate of every pool generator screens every direction to exactly zero, selects nothing and reports converged=True while above the ground energy: measured on two qubits against ZZ - X0 - X1, whose ground energy is -2.2360679774997898, the pool (ry, rz, rx) on wire 0 selects index 0 at a screened gradient of -1.0 from the |00> state and selects nothing from the |++> state. And converged reports why the loop stopped rather than how close the energy came, so a pool of one with a zero tolerance reports True at -1.4142135623730354 and a tolerance exit reports True at -1.4142135623730951, while a run that spent its iteration budget reports False at 0.999999999 -- which is the run furthest from the ground energy, so the flag is an exit test in neither direction. Both readings were previously reachable only by reading the loop, and one of them was reachable only as a torch backward error: a builder that supplies no gradient, or a pool element that adds no dependence at the appended angle, now raises ValueError naming the entry point and the cause instead of RuntimeError: element 0 of tensors does not require grad and does not have a grad_fn. The other is the shape difference the baseline names: the CUDA-Q baseline offers a solver object whose ansatz and optimizer are configuration, and this package offers entry points whose ansatz is a circuit builder the caller supplies, so the two surfaces are not one-to-one even where the mathematics matches. Still absent, each on its own evidence: a solver object carrying a pluggable ansatz registry, any constraint, penalty or slack term, adaptive and multi-angle QAOA variants, a warm start from a classical heuristic, a chemistry front end, and the constrained derivative-free handling that COBYLA gives the baseline's VQE path and that this package's SPSA and Nelder-Mead units do not provide. One absence this row used to name is closed and is corrected here rather than left standing: a cost Hamiltonian for a general QUBO or Ising instance is not missing, because flagquantum.algorithms.qubo already carries qubo_to_ising, ising_to_qubo and max_cut_qubo. One of those absences narrowed without the row moving: the gradient-free route within the QAOA half now exists at the objective level rather than the optimizer level. maxcut_objective returns the very callable run_qaoa minimizes, checked through the same edge list and split into gammas and betas the same way, and it is readable with float() without a backward pass, so SPSAOptimizer and NelderMeadOptimizer -- both already shipped and previously reachable from no solver entry point -- can be handed it. Measured on the one-layer triangle from a flat 0.05 start against the -1.0 optimum, Adam reaches -0.9999997615814209 in 300 steps, SPSA -0.9999911189079285 in 400 steps at 1201 evaluations, and Nelder-Mead -1.0000003576278687 in 706 evaluations; the simplex reaches the optimum while reporting converged=False, because that flag measures the simplex collapsing and not the energy arriving, and the route is asserted on the energy rather than on the flag. It is deliberately not a second optimizer parameter on run_qaoa: an SPSA step is a rate-limited update from two objective values while a simplex is a whole run released at once, so one parameter could not carry both shapes without a dispatch hiding which method ran. What the route is not is a constrained method or a sampled one, so the COBYLA gap, every constraint, penalty and slack term, and the shot-based path all remain absent, and the row stays partial. <br><br>Narrower scope at this status: The baseline ships a solver object per algorithm with the ansatz and the optimizer as configuration, plus a constrained derivative-free optimizer. This package ships the mathematics as entry points over a caller-supplied circuit builder, so the surface shape differs: there is no solver object to configure and no pluggable ansatz registry. Both halves are registered capabilities now -- algorithms_variational_solvers for the QAOA half and algorithms_vqe_solvers for the four VQE entry points -- so what keeps this row partial is the surface shape and the still-absent members rather than an unregistered implementation. A cost Hamiltonian for a general QUBO or Ising instance is present through flagquantum.algorithms.qubo and is no longer a gap this row names. |

A code record can also be read into matrices rather than only into a circuit: css_code_matrices lifts its four blocks into a CssCodeMatrices record, which carries hz, hx, lz and lx together, so a code whose stabilizers are known reaches a code-capacity detector error model on either readout basis without a gadget being built for it and without losing a fault family. A pure check is the case whose second run is empty, so the two emission shapes are one rule and the pure checks' source is byte-identical across the change. flagquantum.qec.ZxxzSurfaceCode is the first record built on it. And its checks are not all of one weight -- a face on the patch's edge spans four qubits and a face in its bulk spans six -- so a single data fault lights three detectors, the model is not graphlike, and the matching decoder refuses the patch exactly as it refuses the Steane model. Both sides are measured at one code, round count and fault rate rather than recorded as a refusal alone. Its ReedMuller15 has since landed as a family of its own, and it is the first record here stated on the Boolean cube rather than on a lattice or on a group and the first whose two family distances are not equal: reed_muller_code punctures the two blocks two degrees apart at the one point naming every variable and takes their duals as the two check families, so a width-four cube returns the fifteen-qubit record with an X distance of seven beside a Z distance of three. Which block states which check family is a convention rather than a fact about the code, and this row states it rather than leaving a reader to infer it from two numbers: exchanging the two blocks is the same code with the two Pauli families renamed, which was measured by rounding both readings through qldpc_code before the rule was written, and the mirrored reading is the one that does not reproduce the sentence this row used to carry. The default bound of three therefore still refuses that code, and it refuses it because three is not a search over the X-type family rather than because the code's distance is not three; a bound of seven returns (7, 3) and a distance of three, and the record states both family distances separately rather than only their smaller. That bound is also the family's cost and the reason this route stops where it does: proving the X-type family's least operator has weight seven means exhausting every subset of weight up to six, which is 942648 subsets over the thirty-one points of width five, 75611760 over the sixty-three of width six and 5434287328 over the hundred and twenty-seven of width seven, each measured. Width four is the smallest cube whose punctured pair states a code at all -- at width three the two duals carry three and six rows over seven points and ten of those eighteen pairs of rows anticommute, so there is no stabilizer group to return -- and width five is the size the family is worth knowing for, thirty-one data qubits carrying eleven logical qubits three errors apart where a lattice patch of the same length carries one. Running it also found the limit this row now records. A mixed check's outcome is deterministic neither at the all-zero preparation nor at a Z-basis readout, so no check of the Z-basis experiment is anchored in either place, and the experiment therefore carries detectors only between syndrome rounds and none at all from a syndrome round to the data. The consequence is a mechanism at every distance that fires no detector and flips the observable -- the readout, merging the logical operator's d wires into one mechanism of probability (1 - (1 - 2p) ** d) / 2 -- whose probability grows with the distance and which no pairing decoder can suppress, because there is no detector to pair. The software half of the surface now exists in flagquantum/remote/realtime, but the microsecond feedback loop itself needs an FPGA and a remote-direct-memory-access capable network interface, so it cannot be closed by software at all and is delivered, if at all, with a hardware partner. ARCH-013 records it as an owned blocked row rather than as a plan. The audit re-measured the two names because both occur in the tree and neither is a transport. `FPGA` occurs in `flagquantum/remote/realtime/` only, where `__init__.py:19` and `protocol.py:16` state it is not here and `channels.py:12` explains that a real channel is an FPGA or NIC implementation living outside this package; the package's own README states the same at its `No transport` bullet. `RDMA` occurs once, as the blocker name `BLOCKER_RDMA_NOT_TESTED` at `flagquantum/runtime/audit/claim_boundary.py:64`, whose own docstring at `:296` says the blocker stands until a log shows a fabric route was used, so the marked value it carries is the string rdma_not_tested -- so the name exists to *withhold* the claim, which is the opposite of supplying the transport. `RoCE` likewise occurs once, as the log marker `_NETWORK_FABRIC_ROCE_MARKER` at `:40`, a string read out of a third-party log rather than a route this package can open. The timing half of the token is therefore exactly as narrow as it says: no part of the timing property is claimed or measured, and `flagquantum/remote/realtime/session.py:8` states the same about the clock and the thread. |
| `realtime_transport` | RoCE and Ethernet realtime transport with a device call channel | unsupported | next | A_nvidia_proprietary | none | Partly closed and still not a transport. The vendor-neutral messaging protocol and the device-call channel seam a transport plugs into now exist in flagquantum/remote/realtime, with the slot framing, payload type system, status convention, and function table specified and exercised offline. What remains absent is the transport itself: RoCE and Ethernet carriage, a ring buffer, a dispatcher, and every timing property, none of which software alone can supply. The row stays unsupported so the dependency-class accounting is not flattered by a protocol that measures nothing. The audit found that every word in the token except `verbs` occurs in the tree, and that none of the occurrences is the transport the token denies. `verbs` occurs zero times. `RDMA` and `RoCE` occur once each, as the blocker name and the log marker cited for the feedback-loop row above. `socket` occurs 15 times and splits into three kinds: `socket.gethostname()` written into a manifest, a checkpoint, or a benchmark record (`flagquantum/runtime/distributed/context.py:227`, `flagquantum/runtime/executors/mps/checkpointing.py:227`, `flagquantum/benchmarking/contract.py:21`, `flagquantum/remote/compute/jiuding.py:236`); the constants `TRANSPORT_ROUTE_SOCKET` and the socket markers at `flagquantum/runtime/audit/claim_boundary.py:36`-`:43`, which exist to read a fabric log; and one real listener, `socket.create_server` at `flagquantum/remote/compute/_workspace_executor.py:297`, which serves a remote compute workspace and is not a QPU fabric. `dispatcher` occurs 12 times and splits into three kinds, none of them an implementation. `flagquantum/remote/realtime/payload.py:16` and its `protocol.py:16` state that no dispatcher is here. Most of the rest describe *the counterparty's* dispatcher -- the out-of-process implementation the protocol is written for, whose failure set `service.py:62` and `channels.py:81` report and whose function table `payload.py:179` is a schema for. And one occurrence is a different word entirely: `flagquantum/runtime/executors/stabilizer/route.py:173` means the in-tree runtime caller that lowers a scene before this funnel samples it. So the token's `no dispatcher` means no dispatcher implementation, and this row is the protocol such an implementation would have to satisfy. |
| `realtime_host_api` | Host API and messaging protocol for realtime control | partial | next | B_open_neutral | `realtime_device_call_messaging` | Partly delivered. The vendor-neutral half is the messaging protocol and the device-call abstraction, and both are now implemented and conformance-checked offline in flagquantum/remote/realtime: a fixed-size slot, a typed payload declared by a handler schema, a function table keyed by a hashed handler name, a status convention, and a channel resolved by name at runtime. What keeps the row at partial rather than supported is the other half of the host-facing surface: the dispatcher, the ring buffer, the function-table launch path, and the occupancy and graph entry points are absent by design, because they belong to the hardware partner and to a device runtime this repository does not own. |
| `realtime_sensor_bridge` | Holoscan sensor bridge integration | unsupported | later | A_nvidia_proprietary | none | Absent and NVIDIA-specific. A FlagOS-family equivalent is the replacement target, and it follows the protocol definition; the protocol now exists, while the sensor bridge and its transport do not, so nothing about this row is closed. |

| `simulator_plugin_admission` | NVQIR CircuitSimulator subclass with a registration macro | partial | now | none | `extension_sdk` | The crossing is landed and exercised; the gap is that nothing installed stands on it. `flagquantum/ecosystem/extensions/admission.py` imports `flagquantum.runtime.backend_registry` and registers one route through the existing `register_backend`, so an extension backend discovered from the `flagquantum.extensions` entry-point group does execute: a third-party backend written against the public extension namespace alone runs through `fq.run`, and a run on it reports `execution_path = admitted_extension_backend` with a state that matches the built-in engine. What the distribution declares is one entry point, `backend.qiskit_aer`, and it predates the route contract: its `execute(program, parameters=None)` is the SDK member rather than the Runtime route, and because both protocols are `runtime_checkable` it passes both `isinstance` checks. Admission now binds the declared call and refuses it by name, so this row is a capability with no conforming occupant rather than a protocol with no crossing, and the refusal is the honest state: a backend that cannot be called as `execute(program, *, options)` is rejected before a plan exists instead of failing inside a planned execution. NVQIR's ABI half is a separate row. The audit checked the token's own phrase against the registry rather than against the tree, because the two say different things. capability-maturity.toml's `extension_sdk` row states that there is no stable C ABI, no out-of-process backend, no per-execution discovery, and no numerical equivalence certification between an admitted backend and the built-in engine, and that row's own `focused_tests` is tests/unit/test_backend_execution_admission.py -- the file whose `test_the_reference_backend_agrees_with_the_builtin_engine` runs all ten declared gates, three controls among them with control above target, and asserts the admitted state against a plain run of the same circuit to 1e-5. So a measurement exists and a certification does not, and the token is a quotation of the second statement rather than a denial of the first. Nothing in admission itself compares numerals: it establishes the protocol member and the call shape, so a backend is admitted on shape and on its negotiated capabilities and its agreement with the built-in engine is not a condition of admission. |
